Hood Heroes – épisode 2 : Than Son, l’i: Hood Heroes – Episode 2: Than Son, the Intervention Worker of Saint-Léonard
« Je viens d’une famille de sept enfants: “I come from a family of seven kids – six boys and one girl. We grew up in a tough environment, with poverty and violence.”
Direction La Zone, à Saint-Léonard. On p: Heading to La Zone, in Saint-Léonard, to meet Than Son Pham, 29, a former intervention worker at the youth organization La Zone and now an addiction intervention worker at Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry secondary school. Although he no longer holds a position at La Zone, Son often comes back to the place that connects him to the young people of Saint-Léonard. So it was only natural that La Converse met him there, along with his former colleagues and some of the youth. They had just finished school and gathered at La Zone. In one of the offices of the youth space, with the sound of young people chatting in the background, Than Son Pham told us his story and explained his work with the youth of Saint-Léonard.
« Je viens d’une famille de sept enfants: “I come from a family of seven kids – six boys and one girl. We grew up in a tough environment, with poverty and violence,” he confides. Son’s behavioural problems began when his parents divorced. He went to two different secondary schools, was placed in a class for students with behavioural difficulties, and even had run-ins with the police and the justice system. “My mother is my inspiration, even though she kicked me out four times when I was young. At the time, I didn’t really understand it, but there was a lesson behind it, and I understood it looking back,” Son adds, concluding that she was always there for him despite everything. “I got expelled from school and ended up in adult education [editor’s note: adult school]. That’s where I got more serious and naturally got on the right path. The stars were aligned for me to follow the path I’m on now. At that time, I had two choices: intervention work or something else… something illegal.”
Originaire du Centre-Sud, dans Ville-Mar: Originally from Centre-Sud, in Ville-Marie, he started working in the community sector at age 17. He first went to the Association sportive et communautaire du Centre-Sud as a kid before becoming an activity leader at that same organization. He then moved from activity leader to intervention worker and held that role for 10 years, until he was 27, just before COVID. During the pandemic, he worked in construction, then returned to intervention work by offering his services to La Zone.
« J’ai vécu une enfance compliquée ; don: “I had a complicated childhood, so I had to put some order in my life and follow the right path – intervention work – where I grew as a human being. I had no role model to lean on. So I tell myself that if I can be that role model to help future generations, all the better,” sums up Son, who naturally wanted to become an intervention worker and sees his work as a logical continuation of what he has lived through.
« J’ai fait deux écoles secondaires, pui: “I went to two secondary schools, then ended up in adult education, and that’s when people told me I’d be good with young people. Why? I have no idea. I was already working with youth, but only one day a week. Once I saw I was having a positive impact on them, I just kept going down that path.” That’s how the story between Son and the youth began. When he was younger, he turned down a chance to play hockey at a high level and chose “the street and money” instead. After that, a different Son was born, thanks to his passion. “I turned down jobs at $28, $30, $35 an hour to do what I do today. I don’t work in intervention for the money, but because I love it. I work because I’m passionate about helping others,” he says. “What I love is seeing a young person’s progress, no matter how they evolve. One of my strengths in intervention is building connections with young people. How do I do it? I don’t know,” he wonders.
En arrivant à La Zone, il a appris à con: When he arrived at La Zone, he got to know the youth of Saint-Léonard, never judging them but giving them advice. “By talking with the young people here so much, they understood I was there for their own good, and they started to trust me. Helping has become my passion. I love what I do, no matter where: at La Zone, at school or at my old job – they can feel that I’m there for the well-being of the people in front of me. I’m here for them.” To sum up his approach, you could say Son listens, understands, listens again, shows patience and, above all, adapts. “Just the fact that they feel understood and listened to, that they tell me about situations I’ve lived through and that they know it, is essential. When they learn about my past, they understand my approach,” he explains, adding that his goal isn’t to change people, but to prevent problems and help them understand the things no one ever helped him understand when he was younger.
« Je ne suis pas d’accord avec le fait q: “I don’t agree with the idea that some people don’t have a passion. You just have to discover it,” the secondary school intervention worker tells us when we ask him about young people who are sometimes “lost” about their future. There’s no better way to illustrate it than an example from his workday: “A young guy came to see me and told me that later on, he didn’t want to do anything, because nothing interested him. Then, as we talked, he and I realized he liked cooking. ‘So cooking is your passion?’ ‘Um… yes.’ And that’s how, by digging and above all by listening to young people, you find their passion.” Passion as a way to stay away from neighbourhood problems, in particular – that is Son’s great motivation, what allowed him to get out and give back to the community. How? “Being there, being a support. Helping young people understand the problems they’re going to face, whatever paths they take. You have to raise their awareness right from the source, that is, well before secondary school, because by then it may already be too late…”
La conscientisation, c’est ce que veut t: Raising awareness is what Than Son Pham wants to pass on to the youth of Saint-Léonard. You have to “awaken their light,” as he puts it so well, before delving deeper into the question of awareness as a legacy.
Mais si on veut vraiment résumer l’histo: But if we really want to sum up Son’s story and his impact on the youth of “Saint-Lô,” the only way to do it is with his own words: “Believe in your dreams, no matter the field. Find a path to stay away from trouble. If you’re not ready to go to prison or get killed for what you’re doing, then don’t do it. If you think you have the shoulders to take on those consequences, that’s your choice. Me, though, I really encourage you to follow your dreams and what you’re passionate about. That’s what will make you live happily your whole life!”
